item.excerpt:encoded: A warm and friendly children's book-style illustration of a single mother sitting at a desk, looking confused as she stares at a computer screen. Her eyebrows are slightly raised, and her mouth is slightly open, showing a puzzled yet determined expression. The cozy home setting in the background includes soft lighting, warm colours, and subtle details like a child playing nearby and a pet sitting beside her, creating a reassuring and relatable atmosphere.

wp:postmeta.wp:meta_value: A colorful and friendly children's illustration of a cheerful single parent sitting with two children at a table, using a laptop. The background is a simple, warm color, keeping the focus on their happy interaction. The style is cartoonish and engaging, designed to be inviting for families and parents.

A father and his young daughter sit together on a sofa, engaged in a heartfelt conversation. The father looks gentle and reassuring, while the daughter listens attentively, reflecting emotions of curiosity and concern. Soft natural lighting enhances the warmth and intimacy of the moment.

A symbolic digital painting of a co-parenting family walking together, with a child holding hands with both parents. Seen from behind, the mother, father, and child walk down a glowing path, surrounded by warm autumn hues. The expressive brushstrokes and vibrant colors evoke a sense of unity, hope, and shared responsibility in raising a child after separation

item.title: Privacy Policy
item.dc:creator: danieljbetts89@gmail.com
item.content:encoded:
Who we are

Suggested text: Our website address is: http://https://thebreakingdad.co.uk.

Comments

Suggested text: When visitors leave comments on the site we collect the data shown in the comments form, and also the visitor’s IP address and browser user agent string to help spam detection.

An anonymized string created from your email address (also called a hash) may be provided to the Gravatar service to see if you are using it. The Gravatar service privacy policy is available here: https://automattic.com/privacy/. After approval of your comment, your profile picture is visible to the public in the context of your comment.

Media

Suggested text: If you upload images to the website, you should avoid uploading images with embedded location data (EXIF GPS) included. Visitors to the website can download and extract any location data from images on the website.

Cookies

Suggested text: If you leave a comment on our site you may opt-in to saving your name, email address and website in cookies. These are for your convenience so that you do not have to fill in your details again when you leave another comment. These cookies will last for one year.

If you visit our login page, we will set a temporary cookie to determine if your browser accepts cookies. This cookie contains no personal data and is discarded when you close your browser.

When you log in, we will also set up several cookies to save your login information and your screen display choices. Login cookies last for two days, and screen options cookies last for a year. If you select "Remember Me", your login will persist for two weeks. If you log out of your account, the login cookies will be removed.

If you edit or publish an article, an additional cookie will be saved in your browser. This cookie includes no personal data and simply indicates the post ID of the article you just edited. It expires after 1 day.

Embedded content from other websites

Suggested text: Articles on this site may include embedded content (e.g. videos, images, articles, etc.). Embedded content from other websites behaves in the exact same way as if the visitor has visited the other website.

These websites may collect data about you, use cookies, embed additional third-party tracking, and monitor your interaction with that embedded content, including tracking your interaction with the embedded content if you have an account and are logged in to that website.

Who we share your data with

Suggested text: If you request a password reset, your IP address will be included in the reset email.

How long we retain your data

Suggested text: If you leave a comment, the comment and its metadata are retained indefinitely. This is so we can recognize and approve any follow-up comments automatically instead of holding them in a moderation queue.

For users that register on our website (if any), we also store the personal information they provide in their user profile. All users can see, edit, or delete their personal information at any time (except they cannot change their username). Website administrators can also see and edit that information.

What rights you have over your data

Suggested text: If you have an account on this site, or have left comments, you can request to receive an exported file of the personal data we hold about you, including any data you have provided to us. You can also request that we erase any personal data we hold about you. This does not include any data we are obliged to keep for administrative, legal, or security purposes.

Where your data is sent

Suggested text: Visitor comments may be checked through an automated spam detection service.

Separated Parents

Navigating parenthood after separation can be overwhelming — but you’re not alone. Whether you're newly separated or facing ongoing challenges, this page offers practical advice and personal stories for parents finding their way after a breakup.

Primary Carer Rights UK: A Guide for Separated Parents

Daniel Betts May 25, 2025 No Comments

Featured: 4 Tips for Coping With Separation

What are my rights as a separated parent in the UK?

As a parent, you have parental responsibility if you're named on the birth certificate or were married to the other parent at the time of the child's birth. This means you have a legal say in important decisions about your child’s upbringing, including education, healthcare, and religion — regardless of who the child lives with.

Do I need a formal agreement to co-parent after separation?

While it’s not a legal requirement, a parenting plan can help avoid conflict. It outlines agreements on contact arrangements, communication, holidays, and more. Parenting plans aren't legally binding but can be formalised through a court order.

What is a child arrangement order?

A Child Arrangement Order is made by the court and decides where a child lives, who they spend time with, and when. It replaces older terms like “custody” and “access” in UK law. It’s typically a last resort if parents can’t agree.

How can we reduce conflict while co-parenting?

Effective communication, consistent routines, and using shared parenting apps can help. Agree on boundaries and prioritise your child’s well-being. Try these tips for dealing with high-conflict co-parenting and, if tension remains high, consider parallel parenting, where contact between parents is minimised.

Can I stop my ex from seeing the children?

Not without a court order. If you have concerns about the child’s safety, speak to a solicitor or contact social services. Otherwise, both parents are typically encouraged to maintain a relationship with the child, even after separation. Mediation can be a great place to start.

What is parallel parenting

Parallel parenting is a style of co-parenting used when communication is high-conflict. Parents disengage from each other and focus solely on their own relationship with the child. Schedules are followed strictly, and communication is kept minimal and business-like.

What support is available for separated dads in the UK?

There are organisations like Families Need Fathers, Dads Unlimited, and local parenting support groups that help separated dads with emotional support, legal advice, and community. Blogs like this (The Breaking Dad) also offer real-life perspectives. Read this if you're struggling, specifically for navigating life as a single father.

How do I tell my children we're separating?

Be age-appropriate, honest, and united (if possible). Reassure them it’s not their fault and explain what’s changing and what’s staying the same. Keep the focus on their needs and answer questions patiently. Read this guide on how to tell your children about divorce or separation if you're struggling. 

Do we need to go to court to sort out contact arrangements?

No — many parents reach an agreement through informal discussion or mediation. Court is typically a last resort when parents can’t agree. Mediation is often required before court applications.

Can I move away with my child after separation?

If the other parent has parental responsibility, you must get their permission to relocate with the child — especially if moving abroad. Without agreement, you may need a court order to proceed. This also applies for travelling abroad on holiday with your child.

Separated Parents

Navigating parenthood after separation can be overwhelming — but you’re not alone. Whether you're newly separated or facing ongoing challenges, this page offers practical advice and personal stories for parents finding their way after a breakup.

Primary Carer Rights UK: A Guide for Separated Parents

Featured: 4 Tips for Coping With Separation

Frequently asked questions

What are my rights as a separated parent in the UK?

As a parent, you have parental responsibility if you're named on the birth certificate or were married to the other parent at the time of the child's birth. This means you have a legal say in important decisions about your child’s upbringing, including education, healthcare, and religion — regardless of who the child lives with.

Do I need a formal agreement to co-parent after separation?

While it’s not a legal requirement, a parenting plan can help avoid conflict. It outlines agreements on contact arrangements, communication, holidays, and more. Parenting plans aren't legally binding but can be formalised through a court order.

What is a child arrangement order?

A Child Arrangement Order is made by the court and decides where a child lives, who they spend time with, and when. It replaces older terms like “custody” and “access” in UK law. It’s typically a last resort if parents can’t agree.

How can we reduce conflict while co-parenting?

Effective communication, consistent routines, and using shared parenting apps can help. Agree on boundaries and prioritise your child’s well-being. Try these tips for dealing with high-conflict co-parenting and, if tension remains high, consider parallel parenting, where contact between parents is minimised.

Can I stop my ex from seeing the children?

Not without a court order. If you have concerns about the child’s safety, speak to a solicitor or contact social services. Otherwise, both parents are typically encouraged to maintain a relationship with the child, even after separation. Mediation can be a great place to start.

What is parallel parenting

Parallel parenting is a style of co-parenting used when communication is high-conflict. Parents disengage from each other and focus solely on their own relationship with the child. Schedules are followed strictly, and communication is kept minimal and business-like.

What support is available for separated dads in the UK?

There are organisations like Families Need Fathers, Dads Unlimited, and local parenting support groups that help separated dads with emotional support, legal advice, and community. Blogs like this (The Breaking Dad) also offer real-life perspectives. Read this if you're struggling, specifically for navigating life as a single father.

How do I tell my children we're separating?

Be age-appropriate, honest, and united (if possible). Reassure them it’s not their fault and explain what’s changing and what’s staying the same. Keep the focus on their needs and answer questions patiently. Read this guide on how to tell your children about divorce or separation if you're struggling. 

Do we need to go to court to sort out contact arrangements?

No — many parents reach an agreement through informal discussion or mediation. Court is typically a last resort when parents can’t agree. Mediation is often required before court applications.

Can I move away with my child after separation?

If the other parent has parental responsibility, you must get their permission to relocate with the child — especially if moving abroad. Without agreement, you may need a court order to proceed. This also applies for travelling abroad on holiday with your child.

Separated Parents

Navigating parenthood after separation can be overwhelming — but you’re not alone. Whether you're newly separated or facing ongoing challenges, this page offers practical advice and personal stories for parents finding their way after a breakup.

Primary Carer Rights UK: A Guide for Separated Parents

Featured: 4 Tips for Coping With Separation

Frequently asked questions

What are my rights as a separated parent in the UK?

As a parent, you have parental responsibility if you're named on the birth certificate or were married to the other parent at the time of the child's birth. This means you have a legal say in important decisions about your child’s upbringing, including education, healthcare, and religion — regardless of who the child lives with.

Do I need a formal agreement to co-parent after separation?

While it’s not a legal requirement, a parenting plan can help avoid conflict. It outlines agreements on contact arrangements, communication, holidays, and more. Parenting plans aren't legally binding but can be formalised through a court order.

What is a child arrangement order?

A Child Arrangement Order is made by the court and decides where a child lives, who they spend time with, and when. It replaces older terms like “custody” and “access” in UK law. It’s typically a last resort if parents can’t agree.

How can we reduce conflict while co-parenting?

Effective communication, consistent routines, and using shared parenting apps can help. Agree on boundaries and prioritise your child’s well-being. Try these tips for dealing with high-conflict co-parenting and, if tension remains high, consider parallel parenting, where contact between parents is minimised.

Can I stop my ex from seeing the children?

Not without a court order. If you have concerns about the child’s safety, speak to a solicitor or contact social services. Otherwise, both parents are typically encouraged to maintain a relationship with the child, even after separation. Mediation can be a great place to start.

What is parallel parenting

Parallel parenting is a style of co-parenting used when communication is high-conflict. Parents disengage from each other and focus solely on their own relationship with the child. Schedules are followed strictly, and communication is kept minimal and business-like.

What support is available for separated dads in the UK?

There are organisations like Families Need Fathers, Dads Unlimited, and local parenting support groups that help separated dads with emotional support, legal advice, and community. Blogs like this (The Breaking Dad) also offer real-life perspectives. Read this if you're struggling, specifically for navigating life as a single father.

How do I tell my children we're separating?

Be age-appropriate, honest, and united (if possible). Reassure them it’s not their fault and explain what’s changing and what’s staying the same. Keep the focus on their needs and answer questions patiently. Read this guide on how to tell your children about divorce or separation if you're struggling. 

Do we need to go to court to sort out contact arrangements?

No — many parents reach an agreement through informal discussion or mediation. Court is typically a last resort when parents can’t agree. Mediation is often required before court applications.

Can I move away with my child after separation?

If the other parent has parental responsibility, you must get their permission to relocate with the child — especially if moving abroad. Without agreement, you may need a court order to proceed. This also applies for travelling abroad on holiday with your child.

asked questions","_padding":{"unit":"px","top":"0","right":"0","bottom":"010","left":"0","isLinked":false},"display_condition_list":[{"display_condition_login_status":"subscriber","_id":"f4b2f07"}]},"elements":[],"widgetType":"heading"},{"id":"335c2eb5","elType":"widget","settings":{"presets_options":"preset-2","tabs":[{"question":"What are my rights as a separated parent in the UK?","answer":"

As a parent, you have parental responsibility if you're named on the birth certificate or were married to the other parent at the time of the child's birth. This means you have a legal say in important decisions about your child\u2019s upbringing, including education, healthcare, and religion \u2014 regardless of who the child lives with.<\/p>","_id":"09323a3"},{"question":"Do I need a formal agreement to co-parent after separation?","answer":"

While it\u2019s not a legal requirement, a parenting plan<\/strong><\/a> can help avoid conflict. It outlines agreements on contact arrangements, communication, holidays, and more. Parenting plans aren't legally binding but can be formalised through a court order.<\/p>","_id":"e8f760f"},{"question":"What is a child arrangement order?","answer":"

A Child Arrangement Order<\/strong> is made by the court and decides where a child lives, who they spend time with, and when. It replaces older terms like \u201ccustody\u201d and \u201caccess\u201d in UK law. It\u2019s typically a last resort if parents can\u2019t agree.<\/p>","_id":"844920c"},{"_id":"1c2fe87","question":"How can we reduce conflict while co-parenting?","answer":"

Effective communication, consistent routines, and using shared parenting apps<\/a> can help. Agree on boundaries and prioritise your child\u2019s well-being. Try these tips for dealing with high-conflict co-parenting<\/a> and, if tension remains high, consider parallel parenting<\/strong><\/a>, where contact between parents is minimised.<\/p>"},{"_id":"17292a6","question":"Can I stop my ex from seeing the children?","answer":"

Not without a court order. If you have concerns about the child\u2019s safety, speak to a solicitor or contact social services. Otherwise, both parents are typically encouraged to maintain a relationship with the child, even after separation. Mediation<\/a> can be a great place to start.<\/p>"},{"_id":"23d2dcd","question":"What is parallel parenting","answer":"

Parallel parenting<\/a> is a style of co-parenting used when communication is high-conflict. Parents disengage from each other and focus solely on their own relationship with the child. Schedules are followed strictly, and communication is kept minimal and business-like.<\/p>"},{"_id":"2b683d4","question":"What support is available for separated dads in the UK?","answer":"

There are organisations like Families Need Fathers<\/strong>, Dads Unlimited<\/strong>, and local parenting support groups that help separated dads with emotional support, legal advice, and community. Blogs like this (The Breaking Dad)<\/em> also offer real-life perspectives. Read this if you're struggling, specifically for navigating life as a single father<\/a>.<\/p>"},{"_id":"a68ae29","question":"How do I tell my children we're separating?","answer":"

Be age-appropriate, honest, and united (if possible). Reassure them it\u2019s not their fault and explain what\u2019s changing and what\u2019s staying the same. Keep the focus on their needs and answer questions patiently. Read this guide on how to tell your children about divorce or separation<\/a> if you're struggling.\u00a0<\/p>"},{"_id":"8d235a8","question":"Do we need to go to court to sort out contact arrangements?","answer":"

No \u2014 many parents reach an agreement through informal discussion or mediation<\/a>. Court is typically a last resort when parents can\u2019t agree. Mediation is often required before court applications.<\/p>"},{"_id":"4f0e0f9","question":"Can I move away with my child after separation?","answer":"

If the other parent has parental responsibility, you must get their permission to relocate with the child \u2014 especially if moving abroad. Without agreement, you may need a court order to proceed. This also applies for travelling abroad on holiday with your child<\/a>.\u00a0<\/p>"}],"enable_toggle_layout":"","row_gap":{"unit":"px","size":15,"sizes":[]},"enable_seperator":"","selected_icon":{"value":"","library":""},"selected_active_icon":{"value":"fas fa-sort-down","library":"fa-solid"},"faq_box_border_style":"none","uael_box_border_width":{"unit":"px","top":"1","right":"1","bottom":"1","left":"1","isLinked":true},"uael_border_radius":{"unit":"px","top":"1","right":"1","bottom":"1","left":"1","isLinked":true},"heading_tag":"h4","uael_title_background":"#F5F5F5","uael_active_title_background":"#E0E0E0","title_padding":{"unit":"px","top":"12","right":"12","bottom":"12","left":"20","isLinked":false},"uael_content_background":"#FCFCFC","uael_content_padding":{"unit":"px","top":"12","right":"12","bottom":"12","left":"12","isLinked":true},"display_condition_list":[{"display_condition_login_status":"subscriber","_id":"076e42f"}],"__globals__":[]},"elements":[],"widgetType":"uael-faq"}],"isInner":false}]

item.title: Sample Page
item.dc:creator: danieljbetts89@gmail.com
item.content:encoded:
This is an example page. It's different from a blog post because it will stay in one place and will show up in your site navigation (in most themes). Most people start with an About page that introduces them to potential site visitors. It might say something like this:

Hi there! I'm a bike messenger by day, aspiring actor by night, and this is my website. I live in Los Angeles, have a great dog named Jack, and I like piña coladas. (And gettin' caught in the rain.)

...or something like this:

The XYZ Doohickey Company was founded in 1971, and has been providing quality doohickeys to the public ever since. Located in Gotham City, XYZ employs over 2,000 people and does all kinds of awesome things for the Gotham community.

As a new WordPress user, you should go to your dashboard to delete this page and create new pages for your content. Have fun!

About The Breaking Dad

Hi, I’m the dad behind The Breaking Dad – a blog about the real, sometimes chaotic, often rewarding adventure of modern family life.

I’m a UK-based father navigating the ups and downs of parenting in a blended family. Here, I share honest stories from my own journey – from the challenges of co-parenting and building strong relationships with my kids and stepkids, to discovering the best family days out, useful parenting tips, and everything in between.

The Breaking Dad is my space to share what I’ve learned, celebrate the good days, and keep it real about the tough ones. Whether you’re looking for practical advice, honest reviews, or just a bit of reassurance that you’re not alone in the madness, you’re in the right place.

Thanks for stopping by – I hope you find something here that helps or inspires you on your own parenting journey.

item.content:encoded:
Separated Parents Support & Advice

Navigating life as a separated parent can be challenging, but you don't have to go through it alone. Whether you're figuring out co-parenting dynamics, dealing with emotional hurdles, or simply looking for practical advice, you’ve come to the right place.

Separated Parents

Navigating parenthood after separation can be overwhelming — but you’re not alone. Whether you're newly separated or facing ongoing challenges, this page offers practical advice and personal stories for parents finding their way after a breakup.

Primary Carer Rights UK: A Guide for Separated Parents

How a parenting plan can help in 2025

The Role of Mediation in Co-parenting: A Comprehensive Guide

Co-Parenting After a Toxic Relationship: A Guide to Positive Parenting

We moved in together!

Featured: 4 Tips for Coping With Separation

Frequently asked questions

What are my rights as a separated parent in the UK?

As a parent, you have parental responsibility if you're named on the birth certificate or were married to the other parent at the time of the child's birth. This means you have a legal say in important decisions about your child’s upbringing, including education, healthcare, and religion — regardless of who the child lives with.

Do I need a formal agreement to co-parent after separation?

While it’s not a legal requirement, a parenting plan can help avoid conflict. It outlines agreements on contact arrangements, communication, holidays, and more. Parenting plans aren't legally binding but can be formalised through a court order.

What is a child arrangement order?

A Child Arrangement Order is made by the court and decides where a child lives, who they spend time with, and when. It replaces older terms like “custody” and “access” in UK law. It’s typically a last resort if parents can’t agree.

How can we reduce conflict while co-parenting?

Effective communication, consistent routines, and using shared parenting apps can help. Agree on boundaries and prioritise your child’s well-being. Try these tips for dealing with high-conflict co-parenting and, if tension remains high, consider parallel parenting, where contact between parents is minimised.

Can I stop my ex from seeing the children?

Not without a court order. If you have concerns about the child’s safety, speak to a solicitor or contact social services. Otherwise, both parents are typically encouraged to maintain a relationship with the child, even after separation. Mediation can be a great place to start.

What is parallel parenting

Parallel parenting is a style of co-parenting used when communication is high-conflict. Parents disengage from each other and focus solely on their own relationship with the child. Schedules are followed strictly, and communication is kept minimal and business-like.

What support is available for separated dads in the UK?

There are organisations like Families Need Fathers, Dads Unlimited, and local parenting support groups that help separated dads with emotional support, legal advice, and community. Blogs like this (The Breaking Dad) also offer real-life perspectives. Read this if you're struggling, specifically for navigating life as a single father.

How do I tell my children we're separating?

Be age-appropriate, honest, and united (if possible). Reassure them it’s not their fault and explain what’s changing and what’s staying the same. Keep the focus on their needs and answer questions patiently. Read this guide on how to tell your children about divorce or separation if you're struggling. 

Do we need to go to court to sort out contact arrangements?

No — many parents reach an agreement through informal discussion or mediation. Court is typically a last resort when parents can’t agree. Mediation is often required before court applications.

Can I move away with my child after separation?

If the other parent has parental responsibility, you must get their permission to relocate with the child — especially if moving abroad. Without agreement, you may need a court order to proceed. This also applies for travelling abroad on holiday with your child.

Frequently asked questions

What are my rights as a separated parent in the UK?

As a parent, you have parental responsibility if you're named on the birth certificate or were married to the other parent at the time of the child's birth. This means you have a legal say in important decisions about your child’s upbringing, including education, healthcare, and religion — regardless of who the child lives with.

Do I need a formal agreement to co-parent after separation?

While it’s not a legal requirement, a parenting plan can help avoid conflict. It outlines agreements on contact arrangements, communication, holidays, and more. Parenting plans aren't legally binding but can be formalised through a court order.

What is a child arrangement order?

A Child Arrangement Order is made by the court and decides where a child lives, who they spend time with, and when. It replaces older terms like “custody” and “access” in UK law. It’s typically a last resort if parents can’t agree.

How can we reduce conflict while co-parenting?

Effective communication, consistent routines, and using shared parenting apps can help. Agree on boundaries and prioritise your child’s well-being. Try these tips for dealing with high-conflict co-parenting and, if tension remains high, consider parallel parenting, where contact between parents is minimised.

Can I stop my ex from seeing the children?

Not without a court order. If you have concerns about the child’s safety, speak to a solicitor or contact social services. Otherwise, both parents are typically encouraged to maintain a relationship with the child, even after separation. Mediation can be a great place to start.

What is parallel parenting

Parallel parenting is a style of co-parenting used when communication is high-conflict. Parents disengage from each other and focus solely on their own relationship with the child. Schedules are followed strictly, and communication is kept minimal and business-like.

What support is available for separated dads in the UK?

There are organisations like Families Need Fathers, Dads Unlimited, and local parenting support groups that help separated dads with emotional support, legal advice, and community. Blogs like this (The Breaking Dad) also offer real-life perspectives. Read this if you're struggling, specifically for navigating life as a single father.

How do I tell my children we're separating?

Be age-appropriate, honest, and united (if possible). Reassure them it’s not their fault and explain what’s changing and what’s staying the same. Keep the focus on their needs and answer questions patiently. Read this guide on how to tell your children about divorce or separation if you're struggling. 

Do we need to go to court to sort out contact arrangements?

No — many parents reach an agreement through informal discussion or mediation. Court is typically a last resort when parents can’t agree. Mediation is often required before court applications.

Can I move away with my child after separation?

If the other parent has parental responsibility, you must get their permission to relocate with the child — especially if moving abroad. Without agreement, you may need a court order to proceed. This also applies for travelling abroad on holiday with your child.

Support and Advice for Separated Parents

Navigating parenthood after separation can be overwhelming — but you’re not alone. Whether you're newly separated or facing ongoing challenges, this page offers practical advice and personal stories for parents finding their way after a breakup.

Child Maintenance Service (CMS) Changes 2025: What UK Parents Need to Know

Daniel Betts June 29, 2025 No Comments

What is Co-Parenting? The Ultimate Guide to Raising Happy Kids After Separation

How to Talk to Kids About Divorce: A Parent’s Guide to a Healthier Transition

What single parent benefits am I entitled to in the UK?

Some of our older content...

Universal Credit for Single Parents: A Complete UK Guide (2025)

Dating for Single Parents: A Practical Guide to Love and Connection

How a parenting plan can help in 2025

The Role of Mediation in Co-parenting: A Comprehensive Guide

Co-Parenting After a Toxic Relationship: A Guide to Positive Parenting

We moved in together!

Frequently asked questions

What are my rights as a separated parent in the UK?

As a parent, you have parental responsibility if you're named on the birth certificate or were married to the other parent at the time of the child's birth. This means you have a legal say in important decisions about your child’s upbringing, including education, healthcare, and religion — regardless of who the child lives with.

Do I need a formal agreement to co-parent after separation?

While it’s not a legal requirement, a parenting plan can help avoid conflict. It outlines agreements on contact arrangements, communication, holidays, and more. Parenting plans aren't legally binding but can be formalised through a court order.

What is a child arrangement order?

A Child Arrangement Order is made by the court and decides where a child lives, who they spend time with, and when. It replaces older terms like “custody” and “access” in UK law. It’s typically a last resort if parents can’t agree.

How can we reduce conflict while co-parenting?

Effective communication, consistent routines, and using shared parenting apps can help. Agree on boundaries and prioritise your child’s well-being. Try these tips for dealing with high-conflict co-parenting and, if tension remains high, consider parallel parenting, where contact between parents is minimised.

Can I stop my ex from seeing the children?

Not without a court order. If you have concerns about the child’s safety, speak to a solicitor or contact social services. Otherwise, both parents are typically encouraged to maintain a relationship with the child, even after separation. Mediation can be a great place to start.

What is parallel parenting

Parallel parenting is a style of co-parenting used when communication is high-conflict. Parents disengage from each other and focus solely on their own relationship with the child. Schedules are followed strictly, and communication is kept minimal and business-like.

What support is available for separated dads in the UK?

There are organisations like Families Need Fathers, Dads Unlimited, and local parenting support groups that help separated dads with emotional support, legal advice, and community. Blogs like this (The Breaking Dad) also offer real-life perspectives. Read this if you're struggling, specifically for navigating life as a single father.

How do I tell my children we're separating?

Be age-appropriate, honest, and united (if possible). Reassure them it’s not their fault and explain what’s changing and what’s staying the same. Keep the focus on their needs and answer questions patiently. Read this guide on how to tell your children about divorce or separation if you're struggling. 

Do we need to go to court to sort out contact arrangements?

No — many parents reach an agreement through informal discussion or mediation. Court is typically a last resort when parents can’t agree. Mediation is often required before court applications.

Can I move away with my child after separation?

If the other parent has parental responsibility, you must get their permission to relocate with the child — especially if moving abroad. Without agreement, you may need a court order to proceed. This also applies for travelling abroad on holiday with your child.

are my rights as a separated parent in the UK?","answer":"

As a parent, you have parental responsibility if you're named on the birth certificate or were married to the other parent at the time of the child's birth. This means you have a legal say in important decisions about your child\u2019s upbringing, including education, healthcare, and religion \u2014 regardless of who the child lives with.<\/p>","_id":"09323a3"},{"question":"Do I need a formal agreement to co-parent after separation?","answer":"

While it\u2019s not a legal requirement, a parenting plan<\/strong><\/a> can help avoid conflict. It outlines agreements on contact arrangements, communication, holidays, and more. Parenting plans aren't legally binding but can be formalised through a court order.<\/p>","_id":"e8f760f"},{"question":"What is a child arrangement order?","answer":"

A Child Arrangement Order<\/strong> is made by the court and decides where a child lives, who they spend time with, and when. It replaces older terms like \u201ccustody\u201d and \u201caccess\u201d in UK law. It\u2019s typically a last resort if parents can\u2019t agree.<\/p>","_id":"844920c"},{"_id":"1c2fe87","question":"How can we reduce conflict while co-parenting?","answer":"

Effective communication, consistent routines, and using shared parenting apps<\/a> can help. Agree on boundaries and prioritise your child\u2019s well-being. Try these tips for dealing with high-conflict co-parenting<\/a> and, if tension remains high, consider parallel parenting<\/strong><\/a>, where contact between parents is minimised.<\/p>"},{"_id":"17292a6","question":"Can I stop my ex from seeing the children?","answer":"

Not without a court order. If you have concerns about the child\u2019s safety, speak to a solicitor or contact social services. Otherwise, both parents are typically encouraged to maintain a relationship with the child, even after separation. Mediation<\/a> can be a great place to start.<\/p>"},{"_id":"23d2dcd","question":"What is parallel parenting","answer":"

Parallel parenting<\/a> is a style of co-parenting used when communication is high-conflict. Parents disengage from each other and focus solely on their own relationship with the child. Schedules are followed strictly, and communication is kept minimal and business-like.<\/p>"},{"_id":"2b683d4","question":"What support is available for separated dads in the UK?","answer":"

Frequently asked questions

What are my rights as a separated parent in the UK?

As a parent, you have parental responsibility if you're named on the birth certificate or were married to the other parent at the time of the child's birth. This means you have a legal say in important decisions about your child’s upbringing, including education, healthcare, and religion — regardless of who the child lives with.

Do I need a formal agreement to co-parent after separation?

While it’s not a legal requirement, a parenting plan can help avoid conflict. It outlines agreements on contact arrangements, communication, holidays, and more. Parenting plans aren't legally binding but can be formalised through a court order.

What is a child arrangement order?

A Child Arrangement Order is made by the court and decides where a child lives, who they spend time with, and when. It replaces older terms like “custody” and “access” in UK law. It’s typically a last resort if parents can’t agree.

How can we reduce conflict while co-parenting?

Effective communication, consistent routines, and using shared parenting apps can help. Agree on boundaries and prioritise your child’s well-being. Try these tips for dealing with high-conflict co-parenting and, if tension remains high, consider parallel parenting, where contact between parents is minimised.

Can I stop my ex from seeing the children?

Not without a court order. If you have concerns about the child’s safety, speak to a solicitor or contact social services. Otherwise, both parents are typically encouraged to maintain a relationship with the child, even after separation. Mediation can be a great place to start.

What is parallel parenting

Parallel parenting is a style of co-parenting used when communication is high-conflict. Parents disengage from each other and focus solely on their own relationship with the child. Schedules are followed strictly, and communication is kept minimal and business-like.

What support is available for separated dads in the UK?

There are organisations like Families Need Fathers, Dads Unlimited, and local parenting support groups that help separated dads with emotional support, legal advice, and community. Blogs like this (The Breaking Dad) also offer real-life perspectives. Read this if you're struggling, specifically for navigating life as a single father.

How do I tell my children we're separating?

Be age-appropriate, honest, and united (if possible). Reassure them it’s not their fault and explain what’s changing and what’s staying the same. Keep the focus on their needs and answer questions patiently. Read this guide on how to tell your children about divorce or separation if you're struggling. 

Do we need to go to court to sort out contact arrangements?

No — many parents reach an agreement through informal discussion or mediation. Court is typically a last resort when parents can’t agree. Mediation is often required before court applications.

Can I move away with my child after separation?

If the other parent has parental responsibility, you must get their permission to relocate with the child — especially if moving abroad. Without agreement, you may need a court order to proceed. This also applies for travelling abroad on holiday with your child.

Try these tips for dealing with high-conflict co-parenting and, if tension remains high, consider parallel parenting, where contact between parents is minimised.

There are organisations like Families Need Fathers, Dads Unlimited, and local parenting support groups that help separated dads with emotional support, legal advice, and community. are my rights as a separated parent in the UK?","answer":"

As a parent, you have parental responsibility if you're named on the birth certificate or were married to the other parent at the time of the child's birth. This means you have a legal say in important decisions about your child\u2019s upbringing, including education, healthcare, and religion \u2014 regardless of who the child lives with.<\/p>","_id":"09323a3"},{"question":"Do I need a formal agreement to co-parent after separation?","answer":"

While it\u2019s not a legal requirement, a parenting plan<\/strong><\/a> can help avoid conflict. It outlines agreements on contact arrangements, communication, holidays, and more. Parenting plans aren't legally binding but can be formalised through a court order.<\/p>","_id":"e8f760f"},{"question":"What is a child arrangement order?","answer":"

A Child Arrangement Order<\/strong> is made by the court and decides where a child lives, who they spend time with, and when. It replaces older terms like \u201ccustody\u201d and \u201caccess\u201d in UK law. It\u2019s typically a last resort if parents can\u2019t agree.<\/p>","_id":"844920c"},{"_id":"1c2fe87","question":"How can we reduce conflict while co-parenting?","answer":"

Effective communication, consistent routines, and using shared parenting apps<\/a> can help. Agree on boundaries and prioritise your child\u2019s well-being. Try these tips for dealing with high-conflict co-parenting<\/a> and, if tension remains high, consider parallel parenting<\/strong><\/a>, where contact between parents is minimised.<\/p>"},{"_id":"17292a6","question":"Can I stop my ex from seeing the children?","answer":"

Not without a court order. If you have concerns about the child\u2019s safety, speak to a solicitor or contact social services. Otherwise, both parents are typically encouraged to maintain a relationship with the child, even after separation. Mediation<\/a> can be a great place to start.<\/p>"},{"_id":"23d2dcd","question":"What is parallel parenting","answer":"

Parallel parenting<\/a> is a style of co-parenting used when communication is high-conflict. Parents disengage from each other and focus solely on their own relationship with the child. Schedules are followed strictly, and communication is kept minimal and business-like.<\/p>"},{"_id":"2b683d4","question":"What support is available for separated dads in the UK?","answer":"

There are organisations like Families Need Fathers<\/strong>, Dads Unlimited<\/strong>, and local parenting support groups that help separated dads with emotional support, legal advice, and community. Blogs like this (The Breaking Dad)<\/em> also offer real-life perspectives. Read this if you're struggling, specifically for navigating life as a single father<\/a>.<\/p>"},{"_id":"a68ae29","question":"How do I tell my children we're separating?","answer":"

Be age-appropriate, honest, and united (if possible). Reassure them it\u2019s not their fault and explain what\u2019s changing and what\u2019s staying the same. Keep the focus on their needs and answer questions patiently. Read this guide on how to tell your children about divorce or separation<\/a> if you're struggling.\u00a0<\/p>"},{"_id":"8d235a8","question":"Do we need to go to court to sort out contact arrangements?","answer":"

No \u2014 many parents reach an agreement through informal discussion or mediation<\/a>. Court is typically a last resort when parents can\u2019t agree. Mediation is often required before court applications.<\/p>"},{"_id":"4f0e0f9","question":"Can I move away with my child after separation?","answer":"

If the other parent has parental responsibility, you must get their permission to relocate with the child \u2014 especially if moving abroad. Without agreement, you may need a court order to proceed. This also applies for travelling abroad on holiday with your child<\/a>.\u00a0<\/p>"}],"enable_toggle_layout":"","row_gap":{"unit":"px","size":15,"sizes":[]},"enable_seperator":"","selected_icon":{"value":"","library":""},"selected_active_icon":{"value":"fas fa-sort-down","library":"fa-solid"},"faq_box_border_style":"none","uael_box_border_width":{"unit":"px","top":"1","right":"1","bottom":"1","left":"1","isLinked":true},"uael_border_radius":{"unit":"px","top":"1","right":"1","bottom":"1","left":"1","isLinked":true},"heading_tag":"h4","uael_title_background":"#F5F5F5","uael_active_title_background":"#E0E0E0","title_padding":{"unit":"px","top":"12","right":"12","bottom":"12","left":"20","isLinked":false},"uael_content_background":"#FCFCFC","uael_content_padding":{"unit":"px","top":"12","right":"12","bottom":"12","left":"12","isLinked":true},"display_condition_list":[{"display_condition_login_status":"subscriber","_id":"076e42f"}],"__globals__":[]},"elements":[],"widgetType":"uael-faq"}],"isInner":false}]

Crazy Life

Hey, I'm Dan. Otherwise known as The Breaking Dad.

I’m Dan – the face behind The Breaking Dad. Alongside my experience in senior marketing roles for national brands, I’ve collaborated with some of the world’s biggest companies to create engaging partnership content and authentic UGC that speaks to real parents.

If you’re a brand that values creativity, connection, and credibility, let’s talk. Let's talk!

How we can help...

User Generated Content (UGC)

|

|

Reviews

|

Podcast Appearances

Some brands we've worked with...

Instagram
Facebook
LinkedIn
Dan's ability to translate complex social strategies into understandable insights is fascinating and his understanding of our business/target audience helps him provide bespoke strategy for our social platforms, WAY more than any agency would.

He's an incredible asset but I wouldn't recommend him to anyone because then we would get less of his precious time. Harrison Chapman Founder

Case Study: Huel

I worked with Consciously Creative, Huel's appointed agency, to deliver a range of User Generated Content (UCG) that delivered big results. Aside from reducing their cost per acquisition by 90%, the campaign achieved:

uplift in purchase value

item.title: Parenting Time Calculator for Separated Parents in the UK​
item.dc:creator: danieljbetts89@gmail.com
item.content:encoded:
Parenting Time Calculator for Separated Parents in the UK

Working out a fair parenting schedule after separation can be stressful and emotional. Our free Parenting Time Calculator helps you quickly and clearly understand how time with your child is shared between households.

Whether you're aiming for a 50/50 split, alternating weekends, or another arrangement, this tool gives you a simple way to plan and visualise your schedule.
